newsitem.title: USA: Poor start for U.S. land conservation plan-critics.
newsitem.headline: Poor start for U.S. land conservation plan-critics.

text.p: The Clinton administration unveiled new operating rules for the largest U.S. conservation programme Wednesday and was quickly accused of potentially squandering benefits that should go to fragile land.

Under the new rules for the Conservation Reserve, up to 240 million acres, or two-thirds, of U.S. cropland would be eligible for enrollment. Created in 1985, the reserve pays farmers an annual rent to idle fragile land for 10 years.
Sceptics said the vast amount of eligible territory meant high-quality land may be accepted while enrollment was denied to highly erodible land or tracts that threaten water quality.

Ferd Hefner of the Sustainable Agriculture Coalition called the situation "a blow to improved environmental targeting" of conservation programmes. The government will face "the inevitable political pressure" to admit land willy-nilly, he said.

The National Grain and Feed Association, a trade group that has warned lax rules could undercut U.S. food production, echoed Hefner in saying the administration's intentions would be tested in a March 3-28 "sign up" for the reserve.

Agriculture Secretary Dan Glickman said his department would be scrupulous in selecting land for the reserve and would keep good land in crop production. "We will enroll only the most environmentally sensitive land," he told a news conference. "This is not going to be a supply management programme."

Allowed to shelter up to 36.4 million acres, the Conservation Reserve is the largest long-term U.S. land retirement plan ever, costing $1.9 billion a year. Tim Searchinger of the Environmental Defence Fund said the reserve would get 90 percent of federal funds for land preservation in the next decade.

Nearly 33 million acres were currently enrolled. Contracts on 22 million acres expire Sept. 30. Some of the land would not be eligible for re-entry, but overall, there was potential for a massive turnover in acreage.

An "environmental benefits index" will be used by the Agriculture Deprtment to winnow land offered by farmers. It will take into account erosion, water quality and wildlife habitat values on each tract as well rental cost, conservation practices that would remain in place after the contract ended, air quality improvements and if land was in a priority zone.
To be considered, land needed an erosion index of eight or higher and to produce a crop twice in the last five years.

The Environmental Working Group said it took a "trust but verify" view of the new rules and Glickman's vows to be a good steward. The 20 million acres in expiring contracts was equal in size to the state of Indiana, it said.
"Needless to say, (the department) must get it right," Ken Cook, president of the conservation group, said.

Agriculture Department calculations said enrollment would dip to 30 million acres in 1998 and rebound to the 36.4 million-acre ceiling by decade's end. There would be no substantial shifts in acreage among the major crop regions but the Northern Plains, with its "prairie potholes" would gain two million acres in enrollment.
Sen. Pat Roberts, R-Kan., said he was worried there would be too little time before planting season for farmers to learn if land would be accepted for the reserve.
